item.description:
One row is one thing

Wortel 2026.38.3 · 2026-09-14

A command that starts two servers is two rows. bun dev fanning out to dev:web and dev:images puts both of them in one process group, and Wortel was treating a process group as one job. That is true when a shell starts it, and it is how an agent’s jobs arrive, which is why it held up for so long. It is false here: the pair came out as a single row named after whichever started first, carrying their combined memory and showing only the lower of the two ports, with nothing to say the second one existed.

The hidden port was the smaller half of it. That row’s Quit would have stopped both servers, from a row naming one. A process group is now split into the separate trees it contains, so each server is its own row, with its own port and its own Quit. A job that is the whole of its group is still stopped as a group; one sharing a group stops only its own processes.

Pointing at one row no longer highlights several. The highlight was keyed on the process group, which stopped being unique the moment a group could hold more than one job. The same mistake had reached one other place: quitting a row would have taken its neighbour’s row away while that server kept running.

The cursor stays an arrow. It was turning into a pointing hand over a row, which is a web habit. macOS keeps the arrow over clickable rows and says “this does something” with the highlight.

The scan is twice as fast. It was slower than reading everything about every process on the machine, which is a good sign that something is being done twice, and three things were. Abandoned processes were fully inspected before being filtered on the directory that discarded nearly all of them, so the cheap question is asked first now. Whether a process belonged to a session was recomputed once per session rather than once. And each process had its command line read twice, once to recognise an agent and once to name a job.

The list reads properly with VoiceOver. A row was four separate fragments; it is one sentence now, with the port announced as a port, and each Quit says what it stops rather than being one of several identical buttons. The green dot is marked as decoration, because what it means is already in the sentence, and it uses the system green, which follows Increase Contrast.

The running list, read properly

Wortel 2026.38.2 · 2026-09-14

A port is no longer squeezed out of shape. :13337 rendered stacked one digit per line down the row, because the job’s name claimed the row’s width and left the port nothing to lay out in. An address cannot be split, so it takes its width first now, and the name, which is the only thing on the row that can usefully shrink, is what gives way.

Long commands truncate where you can still read them. They were shortened from the middle, which turned quick.js serve dist --dir ... into quick.js serve di...-chat-prototype. A command reads from the left, so it now keeps its beginning. The same goes for a session heading, which is sometimes a whole sentence, because a session can be named from the first thing you typed into it.

Abandoned processes have to be worth mentioning. A chrome_crashpad_handler sitting in a project directory at 2.8 MB is not a server anybody forgot to stop, and it was being listed as one. Something with no session left now has to be holding a port you could reach, or be big enough that stopping it is the point. Your own sessions’ jobs are still listed whatever they cost, because you started them and they are still yours.

One icon in the toolbar, and it stays the same. It used to swap between two different symbols depending on whether anything was serving a port, which made the item harder to find and encoded a distinction the list already draws far better, with a dot and a port on every row. The icon only appears when something is running, so it has nothing left to say beyond that.

What your sessions left running

Wortel 2026.38.1 · 2026-09-14

Wortel shows what each session is still running. A new item appears in the toolbar when there is something to show, and opens a list grouped by session: one row per job, the port it is serving on, what it costs in memory, and a Quit that appears when you point at it. Click a row to open it in your browser, or right-click for Copy Address, Reveal in Finder and Quit. The item is absent, not greyed out, when nothing is running, so a terminal that has started nothing carries no extra chrome.

It reports memory the way Activity Monitor does, which turns out to matter more than it sounds. ps reported a live vite process at 30 MB while it was really holding 572 MB: on a machine under pressure, compressed and swapped pages leave the resident set, and the number every other tool shows you is the one that hides the problem. One session on the machine this was built against was holding 1.39 GB across two dev servers and an agent.

It finds the ones nothing else can. A dev server that outlives its session reparents itself to launchd and keeps nothing pointing back at the terminal that started it, so no tool on your Mac can tell you it is yours. Wortel can, because the working directory still answers days later. Two were sitting on the development machine while this was written: a wrangler four days old holding 399 MB, and a bun script five days old. Neither was serving anything reachable. They appear under “Not attached to a session”, with how long they have been there and which project they came out of.

Closing a session says what it will stop. The warning used to read “A process is still running in this session”, which is equally true of a session holding one sleep and one holding 1.4 GB across two dev servers. Now it names them: “Still running: bun dev:web (:3000), claude, bun dev:images. Closing stops 8 processes and frees 1.05 GB.” The agent is named too, because closing the session does stop it, and that is the part worth reading.

Your agent is never offered a Quit button, and neither is the session’s own shell. What counts as one job is the process group, which is how shells actually work rather than a guess about which processes belong together.

Notifications carry the session’s current name. A notification was posted with the session’s name and the session was often renamed moments later, when the on-device namer or the agent’s own title came back a few seconds after the turn ended. The banner then said “Session 3” while the sidebar said what the work actually was, which reads as a notification about some other session. A renamed session now rewrites its own banner in place, without a second ding.

Two ways a terminal could come back blank. A session restored from a previous launch could fail to take the keyboard, leaving a window that draws but will not accept a keystroke, with nothing on screen saying why. And a session whose program sat idle while the app was closed had nothing to replay and nothing to prompt a repaint, so it came back empty until you touched it. Both are fixed.

The git panel can pull. Fetch told you that you were behind and then left you to go and type the obvious command. Pull sits between fetch and push, and is fast-forward only: a panel with no conflict UI has no business starting a merge it cannot finish, so a diverged branch gets git’s own refusal and the terminal is right there to resolve it in.

Image diffs say what the change costs. An image commit is reviewed on two things, what changed and what it weighs, and the caption only ever had the first. A PNG that gained 400 KB without visibly changing looked like no change at all. Both sides now show their size alongside their dimensions.

Worktree sessions stop inventing a folder. A session’s folder is the part of its name before the last slash, so naming a worktree session after its branch filed it under a folder named for the branch’s namespace: a second sidebar group holding exactly the sessions that belonged in the first one. New sessions are named for the branch’s leaf, and any session already filed in a phantom folder moves back on this launch.

Two new anonymous events come with this release, both counts only: that the running list was opened, with rough numbers of jobs and of processes that had outlived their session, and that something was quit from it. Never what they are, what they are serving, or where they are running. The full list is on the privacy page, which remains the whole list.
